dimensions.anchor_range:
CODEC LAYER (PDU encode/decode, single core, JMH, NO network I/O): smpp-core on Java 21 / Apple M4 reports encodeSubmitSm 1,534,219 ops/s (~650 ns), decodeSubmitSm 1,823,456 ops/s (~550 ns), codec round-trip 751,234 ops/s [medium, vendor JMH, reproducible]. This is the only modern clean-room JVM SMPP codec anchor; Cloudhopper/jSMPP have no credible primary benchmark (the ~70 msg/s jSMPP figure is a competitor's unsourced claim).

FULL TCP submit_sm ROUND-TRIP (single thread, loopback, real client+server+PDUs, NO TLS): smpp-core 25,090 ops/s [medium, single-author]; smpp.com emgload->emgsink native C ~25,000 MPS on 3.0 GHz Xeon [medium, vendor utility] — two independent stacks converge on ~25K. Codec is ~60x faster than network, so codec is never the relay bottleneck.

RELAY/PROXY (stateless two-leg splice with mTLS, both legs): NO published benchmark exists anywhere. This is the central gap.

NETTY-APP CEILINGS (calibration context, not SMPP): MockServer (mature Netty app, 6 pinned cores, ZGC, 8 GB, full logging) saturates ~36,000 req/s with sub-ms p50 / ~0.5 ms p99 [high]; Netty 256B echo loopback ~47K round-trip msg/s, ~21 us one-way [medium, vendor]; Netty + Solarflare Onload kernel-bypass ~2.4M req/s [medium, vendor ceiling].

CARRIER-SIDE PRODUCTION CEILINGS (what actually governs real traffic): Sinch default 10 MT MPS per bind [high]; Twilio up to 400 MPS account-level, short-code 100 MPS, long-code 1 MPS [high]; 8x8 50 MPS per bind default x 4 binds/system_id = ~200 MPS realistic per system_id [high]. Production throughput is 1-3 orders of magnitude below any modern relay's codec ceiling.

MISCONFIGURATION FLOOR: Cloudhopper issue #39 ~200 msg/s with mixed SMSC delays [low, user-reported, not a ceiling]; RestComm JVM SMSC + Cassandra ~1,420-1,601 MPS [medium, conflates persistence].

THEORETICAL per-connection ceiling: ~51,200 msg/s at 512-slot window + 10 ms SMSC latency (Little's Law) [medium, arithmetic, not measured].
dimensions.gaps: No public benchmark exists for an SMPP PROXY/STATELESS RELAY specifically — every SMPP number is a client<->server library (smpp-core, jSMPP, Cloudhopper) doing PDU codec or single-session round-trip. A two-leg splice with mTLS on both legs has zero published reference; Companions would be among the first to publish one. No JVM SMPP codec number on JDK 25 (smpp-core is Java 21; Cloudhopper is Java 8 / Netty 3). No multi-connection or pooled-connection submit_sm/sec — every number is single-connection/single-thread. No mTLS-on-the-wire throughput penalty published for any JVM SMPP stack (directly relevant; smpp-core claims TLS support but publishes no TLS-vs-plaintext delta). No payload-size-sensitivity data (160B vs 256B vs 1KB short_message). No CPU/core scaling curve (1/2/4/8 cores). smpp-core is single-author, ~2 GitHub stars, no third-party replication — treat its 25K as the best available but unreplicated. No credible primary jSMPP benchmark (the ~70 msg/s figure is unsourced competitor marketing). Cloudhopper has NO public throughput number of its own in any credible source — only characterized indirectly via smpp-core's comparison claims.
dimensions.suggested_target:
SUGGESTION (clearly mine, not a source) for a solo OSS portfolio v1:

(1) CODEC MICROBENCH (JMH, single core, no I/O) — target 3x10^5 - 1.5x10^6 encode ops/s and 5x10^5 - 1.8x10^6 decode ops/s per core (~500-700 ns latency). smpp-core on Java 21 already shows 1.5M/1.8M; a clean-room JDK 25 + Netty 4 codec should land in the same order of magnitude. This is the craft-level headline number; publish encode/decode latency in nanoseconds.

(2) END-TO-END STATELESS RELAY (single instance, real loopback/local-sink TCP, mTLS on BOTH legs, OIDC auth cached, virtual-thread relay) — target SUSTAINED >=10,000 submit_sm/sec with a stretch goal of ~25,000/sec. Reasoning: (a) the codec will not be the bottleneck (it is ~60x faster than the network path); (b) 10K is 1-2 orders of magnitude above the commercial peer ceilings that actually govern production (Sinch 10/bind, Twilio <=400/account, 8x8 ~200/system_id), so carrier bind provisioning — not Companions — sets real-world throughput; (c) 25K reaches parity with the modern-Java-SMPP lane (smpp-core 25K single-thread; emgload ~25K). Expect mTLS on two legs and OIDC delegation to subtract from the 25K single-leg figure; budget for the relay itself to be CPU-non-bound at 10K+ and gated by SMSC latency + window size.

(3) PER-CONNECTION PLANNING CEILING (label as theoretical, not a target): ~50K msg/s at 512-slot window + 10 ms SMSC latency (Little's Law).

(4) PRODUCTION SIZING: target '>= N x slowest-peer-bind MPS' where N = bind count, not a fixed number.

Honest ceiling to NOT exceed in claims without a published harness: ~25-36K. MockServer (mature Netty app on 6 cores) saturates near 36K; smpp-core's full TCP round-trip is 25K. Claiming >50K end-to-end without a reproducible percentile-table harness would read as overreach.

dimensions.anchor_range:
VIRTUAL-THREAD FEASIBILITY ENVELOPE: JEP 444 states 1,000,000 virtual threads are supported; on a 1-second-sleep workload a 200-thread platform pool achieves ~200 tasks/sec while VTs achieve ~10,000 tasks/sec, scaling to ~1,000,000 tasks/sec at 1M concurrent VTs [high, JEP 444]. pkolaczk: Java 21-ea VT at 1M tasks beat Go goroutines by ~2x on memory (chart-only exact GB) [medium].

PLATFORM-THREAD COST (the contrast that makes VTs the story): each platform thread reserves ~1 MB stack on Linux x64 (32-64 KB committed) [high, JEP 444 + Oracle Java Magazine + HappyCoders]; 10,000 platform threads ~= 250 MB committed (pkolaczk) / ~10 GB reserved (JEP framing); pkolaczk could NOT launch 100,000 platform threads [medium].

VT FOOTPRINT: initial 'a few hundred bytes', growing to a few KB for shallow I/O-bound stacks; stacks are heap-resident 'stack chunk' objects that grow/shrink [high, JEP 444].

MAX CONCURRENT TCP ON ONE JVM (plain NIO, not Netty/VT): 840,000 concurrent connections on 8 GB Linux (AMD FX-6300 6-core), ~1,602 MB RAM, requiring fs.nr_open=33M + multiple loopback client IPs [medium, Joseph Mate]. WhatsApp canonical reference: 2,000,000+ concurrent TCP on one server (Erlang/OTP/FreeBSD) [high, vendor blog].

VT-ON-NETTY (closest methodological analog to Companions, JDK 25): chrisgleissner/loom-webflux — Spring Boot 4.1 / Corretto 25.0.3 / Netty — VT-Netty accepted every fixed-rate burst up to 60,000 simultaneous connections with zero errors (vs WebFlux-Netty which degraded) [high, reproducible].

NETTY IDLE-CONNECTION CPU (anecdotal floor): single Netty node held ~50,000+ idle WebSocket connections under 5% CPU [low, single Medium post, no methodology].

SMPP PRODUCTION CONCURRENCY (what real traffic actually needs): 2-4 concurrent binds per system_id is the carrier default — 8x8 'baseline of 4 concurrent binds per system_id' [high]; Vonage up to 2 concurrent by default [high]; seven.io max 2 sessions [high]. Real production concurrency is in the TENS to LOW HUNDREDS, not millions.
dimensions.gaps: No published benchmark combines Netty + virtual threads at high connection counts with concrete memory/CPU numbers as a single connection-scaling unit. Critical architectural nuance: Netty's NioEventLoopGroup uses FIXED platform threads (default = 2x CPU cores) for I/O event loops; virtual threads live only in the channel-handler/app-orchestration layer. The two technologies sit at different layers, and no canonical benchmark measures them together. No credible source for concurrent SMPP-bind count or memory on any JVM/Netty SMPP proxy — SMPP binds are typically 1 per system_id per direction. The 'low resource at high concurrency' thesis is real but somewhat ORTHOGONAL to actual SMPP traffic patterns (tens-hundreds of binds, not millions); no SMPP-specific anchor exists. No authoritative RSS figure for a Netty relay at N concurrent connections (heavily tuning-dependent: SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF, allocator, GC). No JDK 25-specific per-VT memory number (JEP 444 / JDK 21 figures remain canonical; JEP 491 in JDK 24 removed synchronized-pinning but did not change per-VT footprint). No credible CPU-utilization figure for a Netty instance holding N IDLE connections (the SMPP steady state).
dimensions.suggested_target:
SUGGESTION (mine, not a source) — set TWO concurrency targets so the craft thesis is demonstrated without overclaiming production need:

HEADLINE / DEMONSTRATED (the portfolio flex): 10,000 concurrent idle SMPP ESME<->proxy<->SMSC socket pairs held in <1 GB JVM heap and <1 vCPU idle, with Netty NioEventLoopGroup (2x CPU cores platform threads) driving the wire and virtual threads used for per-connection blocking orchestration. This is well within the JEP 444 feasibility envelope (1M VT; pkolaczk sub-GB Java-VT-at-1M; chrisgleissner 60K conns on VT-Netty with zero errors) and well above any realistic SMPP production need.

REALISTIC PRODUCTION: 1,000-2,000 concurrent bindings, <256 MB heap, negligible idle CPU — honest for actual SMPP traffic (carrier defaults are 2-4 binds/system_id).

DEFER the 'millions of connections' claim — it requires WhatsApp-grade kernel tuning (fs.nr_open, multiple client IPs to dodge the 65K ephemeral-port limit) that is out of scope for v1. Use a shared PooledByteBufAllocator (NOT per-channel), keep synchronized out of the hot path or rely on JEP 491 (JDK 24+/25), avoid -XX:+PreserveFramePointer, and instrument with ByteBufAllocatorMetric + JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events (threshold 20 ms, on by default).

dimensions.anchor_range:
CODEC (per-PDU, single core): ~550 ns decode, ~650 ns encode, ~1.3 us codec round-trip (smpp-core JMH) [medium]. Negligible vs network.

NETTY ECHO LOOPBACK (256B, two JVMs, 1M warmup + 1M measured): Netty avg 21.17 us one-way, p99 29.7 us, p99.99 55.7 us, max 10.3 ms [medium, vendor CoralBlocks]. Implied ~47K round-trip msg/s ceiling on a single connection.

NETTY-APP MEDIAN/p99 (MockServer, 6 cores, ZGC): sub-ms median up to 16,000 req/s (p99 ~0.5 ms); sub-ms median through 32,000 req/s; saturates ~36,000 req/s [high].

TLS HANDSHAKE — RTT MODEL: TLS 1.2 = 2-RTT, TLS 1.3 = 1-RTT, TLS 1.3 0-RTT resumption = 0-RTT [high, Cloudflare]. TLS 1.3 reduces handshake latency ~35-40% vs 1.2 [medium, two sources].

TLS HANDSHAKE — CPU (loopback, RTT-excluded): ~150 us full-handshake CPU (IBM CICS z/OS) [high]; kernel-TLS 134-307 us min/avg on 1-vCPU VM [high, NetDev academic]. So loopback TLS handshake is hundreds-of-us of CPU.

TLS HANDSHAKE — OVER NETWORK: 20-120 ms median (Heroku SNI Erlang case, reduced 4-5x after cert-cache fix) [medium]; dominated by network RTT + cert handling, not crypto.

mTLS OVERHEAD vs one-way TLS: +1-2 ms CPU, scaling with client-cert chain depth; NO extra round-trip in TLS 1.3 (client Certificate+CertificateVerify ride in the existing post-ServerHello flight) [medium, APISIX + RFC 8446 derivation].

OIDC — Keycloak 26.4 (named reference IdP) login p99: 47 ms @ 0 ms added RT, 84 ms @ 10 ms RT, 130 ms @ 20 ms RT (AWS eu-west-1 cross-AZ); capacity 1 vCPU ~= 15 logins/sec, ~= 120 refresh-token req/sec [high, official vendor benchmark Oct 2025].

OIDC — TOKEN INTROSPECTION (remote, warm+pooled): ~200 ms worked example (commercetools) [medium]; cold/unpooled or serverless >5 s (TLS + pool warm-up) [medium, community]. No introspection-specific Keycloak benchmark (login is a conservative ceiling).

OIDC — LOCAL JWT VERIFY (cached JWKS, the preferred bind path): RS256 verify 0.7-1.2 ms typical, spikes 5-6 ms under GC; cached verified-signature ~0.4-0.6 ms; typically 10-15% of total request latency [medium].

JWKS FETCH: 20-40 ms uncached (cache miss); 2-3 ms with conditional GET; Auth0 notes ~150 ms is not unusual; cache validity ~12 h (IBM) [medium, two sources]. Key-rotation stampede can spike per-token verify 3-4 ms -> 45 ms and gateway latency 18 ms -> 250 ms.

USERINFO ENDPOINT: no published ms SLA for any major IdP; Microsoft Entra recommends using ID-token claims directly to avoid 1-2 extra network RTTs [high, vendor guidance].
dimensions.gaps: No JVM/Netty/JDK-25 loopback TLS handshake microbenchmark (us/handshake, handshakes/sec per core). Only proxies exist: IBM CICS ~150 us (z/OS), kernel-TLS 134-307 us (NetDev, not JVM), Erlang SNI 20-120 ms (over network). Netty only states OpenSSL-backed (tcnative/BoringSSL) is '~3x faster than JDK SSLEngine' without absolutes. This is the single most useful missing anchor for a Netty portfolio piece — should be SELF-MEASURED with JMH rather than cited. No authoritative OIDC UserInfo latency (p50/p99) for any major IdP — only qualitative 'costs 1-2 extra RTTs' guidance. No token-introspection-specific (vs login/refresh) Keycloak benchmark — introspection is lighter (session/cache lookup vs credentials+DB+session) so login numbers are a conservative ceiling, but the exact figure is unpublished. No mTLS handshake cost delta measured on JVM/Netty (APISIX '1-2 ms' is a vendor blog claim without harness; protocol fact is derivable from RFC 8446 but unmeasured publicly; effect scales linearly with client-cert chain depth, also unmeasured). No concrete egress TLS-handshake latency proxy->carrier-SMSC (deployment-specific; reduces to standard 1-RTT TLS 1.3 + crypto model).
dimensions.suggested_target:
SUGGESTION (mine, not a source) — present the bind path as a DECOMPOSED CHAIN, not a single number, because that is the honest shape:

1. Ingress TLS handshake (legacy->proxy): ~1xRTT + 0.3-1 ms crypto (TLS 1.3). LAN/intra-AZ ~1-3 ms; internet ~20-100 ms.
2. mTLS (Mode C): +1-2 ms CPU, no extra RTT in TLS 1.3; scales with client-cert chain depth.
3. OIDC validation — prefer LOCAL JWT via cached JWKS for steady-state binds (~1-5 ms). Remote introspection (warm, pooled, co-located IdP) ~50-100 ms processing + 1xRTT. Cold/uncached (first bind after rotation, or cross-region IdP) ~150 ms-2 s; design fail-closed timeout ~2-5 s.
4. Egress TLS handshake (proxy->SMSC): ~1xRTT + crypto, same model as ingress.

HEADLINE TARGET TO PIN IN THE PRD: 'p99 bind latency <= ~250 ms on the warm path (co-located IdP, TLS 1.3, pooled egress), with an explicit cold-path allowance of <= ~2 s that fail-closes to DENY beyond a configured timeout.' Consistent with Keycloak 26.4 measured login p99 (47 ms @ 0 RTT, 130 ms @ 20 ms RTT) plus one TLS handshake. Mark NOTIONAL and require self-measurement against a mock SMSC + Keycloak (no published benchmark matches this exact stack).

STEADY-STATE PER-PDU RELAY added latency: target sub-ms (codec ~1 us + Netty splice; the SMSC round-trip dominates). Do NOT promise sub-ms bind latency — the bind path includes TLS + OIDC and is dominated by external RTTs.

dimensions.anchor_range:
PLATFORM-THREAD FOOTPRINT: ~1 MB stack reserved per thread on Linux x64, 32-64 KB committed upfront [high, JEP 444 + Oracle Java Magazine + HappyCoders]. 10,000 platform threads ~= 250 MB committed (pkolaczk Xeon E3-1505M v6, Ubuntu 22.04) [medium]; 100,000 platform threads unlaunchable on the same box [medium].

VIRTUAL-THREAD FOOTPRINT: initial 'a few hundred bytes', growing to a few KB for shallow I/O-bound stacks; stacks are heap-resident stack-chunk objects that grow/shrink, upper bound ~half G1 region size (>=512 KB -> StackOverflowError) [high, JEP 444]. 1,000,000 VTs feasible; Java 21-ea VT at 1M tasks beat Go goroutines ~2x on memory (lost to Rust tokio) [medium, pkolaczk].

MAX TCP / RSS ON ONE JVM: 840,000 concurrent TCP connections on 8 GB Linux desktop using ~1,602 MB RAM (19.6% of 8 GB), plain Java NIO (not Netty, not VT); required fs.nr_open=33M + many loopback client IPs [medium, Joseph Mate].

JVM STARTUP / IMAGE FOOTPRINT (VT-based server): jlink modular runtime ~57 MB image, 101 ms startup (JDK HTTP server, Java 21, 8 vCPU c5.2xlarge, 117,448 req/s hello-world); GraalVM native-image ~18 MB binary, 3 ms startup, ~90% of JIT throughput (105,838 req/s) [high, reproducible, ebarlas].

NETTY POOLED-BUFFER FOOTPRINT: PooledByteBufAllocator manages 16 MB PoolChunks; observed ~16 MB on-heap per Netty event-loop thread (Spark at up to 8 threads); up to 2.4 GB direct (off-heap) memory observed via usedDirectMemory() with default allocator settings (gRPC-io) [medium, AutoMQ + Spark SPARK-24938 + gRPC-io]. Pool is amortized across connections — share ONE allocator across all channels.

REFERENCE HARDWARE/HEAP DISCLOSURES (the disclosure bar): MockServer (Netty app) — 6 pinned cores, ZGC, 8 GB heap [high]; chrisgleissner loom-webflux (JDK 25 + VT-Netty) — Intel i5-14600K 14c/20t, 64 GiB DDR5, 2 GiB heap, host rebooted before each run [high].

JDK 24/25 NOTE: JEP 491 (JDK 24, in JDK 25 GA) removed virtual-thread pinning inside synchronized blocks/methods — synchronized-based third-party code no longer pins carriers [high, JEP 444 + JEP 491].
dimensions.gaps: No published RSS / resident-set for a Netty + virtual-thread relay at N concurrent connections — heavily deployment- and tuning-dependent (SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF sizes, allocator config, GC choice); no vendor or reputable benchmark publishes a single number. No canonical benchmark measures Netty + VT TOGETHER as a resource unit (Netty event loops are fixed platform threads; VTs live in the handler layer). No authoritative figure for JVM RSS of a Netty relay at N concurrent connections. No JDK 25-specific per-VT memory number (JEP 444/JDK 21 figures remain canonical; JEP 491 did not change per-VT footprint). No credible CPU-utilization figure for a Netty instance holding N IDLE connections (the SMPP-relay steady state) — expected near-zero but unpublished. Micrometer/observability overhead on a hot SMPP relay path is not publicly benchmarked (relevant to the 'observable via Micrometer' claim).
dimensions.suggested_target:
SUGGESTION (mine, not a source) — resource envelope for a single-instance Companions v1 SMPP MT relay:

HARDWARE/HEAP TARGET: single instance on 4-8 vCPU modern x86/ARM, JDK 25 GA, ZGC, 2-4 GiB heap (aligns with MockServer 8 GB/6 cores and loom-webflux 2 GiB disclosure norms).

CONCURRENCY/RSS DEMO TARGET (the craft flex): 10,000 concurrent idle ESME<->proxy<->SMSC socket pairs held in <1 GB JVM heap and <1 vCPU idle. Defensible within the JEP 444 envelope (1M VT supported; pkolaczk sub-GB at 1M; chrisgleissner 60K VT-Netty conns with zero errors).

DOCKER IMAGE / STARTUP: target ~50-100 MB jlink modular image with <500 ms cold-start, OR ~20 MB GraalVM native-image with <50 ms cold-start (ebarlas shows 57 MB/101 ms jlink and 18 MB/3 ms native are achievable on JDK 21; JDK 25 AOT/CDS should match or improve).

ALLOCATOR DISCIPLINE: ONE shared PooledByteBufAllocator across all channels (avoid per-channel allocators that multiply the ~16 MB/thread footprint); size direct memory explicitly via -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize; expose ByteBufAllocatorMetric for visibility.

VT HYGIENE on JDK 25: rely on JEP 491 (synchronized no longer pins in JDK 24+/25), but still avoid -XX:+PreserveFramePointer ('drastic negative impact' per JEP 444) and verify pinning is absent via JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events (threshold 20 ms).

IDLE-STATE PROOF: publish '<N% CPU at 10K idle connections on <hardware>' as a self-measured artifact (no source exists to borrow from).

workload_context:
Typical SMPP proxy workload shape (so all throughput/concurrency/latency numbers are interpretable): Companions relays MT submit-path traffic + DLRs between a legacy SMPP 3.4 system and a carrier SMSC, as a stateless socket-splice relay with mTLS on both legs and auth delegated to an OIDC authority.

PDU SIZE CORNERS (model at three explicit corners; no single 'average' is sourced): (1) small/typical MT = GSM-7 single SMS, submit_sm ~180-210 bytes on the wire (16 B header + ~25 B addressing/flags + 160 B short_message); (2) UCS-2 single SMS, submit_sm ~180 B (140 B TPDU payload, 70 chars); (3) long-message burst = UCS-2 message split across 3 segments via 6-byte UDH = 3 submit_sm PDUs each ~150 B (per-segment 67 UCS-2 chars), plus matching deliver_sm DLRs. SMPP submit_sm sm_length max = 254 bytes; on-wire SMS TPDU limit = 140 bytes.

BINDS: persistent and long-lived (kept open indefinitely via enquire_link, NOT torn down per-message; rebind is failure-driven, not workload-driven). Carrier defaults bracket at 2-4 concurrent binds per system_id — 8x8 'baseline of 4 concurrent binds per system_id' [high], Vonage up to 2 by default [high], seven.io max 2 sessions [high]. Split TX/RX into dedicated transmitter+receiver binds to avoid head-of-line blocking between submit_sm and deliver_sm (8x8 guidance). Real production concurrency is in the tens to low hundreds of binds total, NOT millions.

PER-BIND THROUGHPUT: 8x8 50 MPS per bind default [high] -> realistic 100-200 MPS sustained per system_id at default provisioning; higher with carrier uplift. Carrier ceilings (Sinch 10 MPS/bind default, Twilio up to 400 MPS account-level) sit 1-3 orders of magnitude below any modern relay's codec ceiling, so the carrier bind — not Companions — governs real-world throughput.

KEEP-ALIVE: emit enquire_link at 30 s (de-facto standard across OpenMarket/360nrs/Infobip/Wavix); declare session dead at ~60 s; rebind wait ~60 s to avoid bind storms (360nrs).

DLR RATIO: configuration-driven via registered_delivery (1 -> ~1 DLR per submit_sm; 0 -> none) per smpp.org; there is NO sourced real-world DLR:MT ratio (a '70-98%' figure floating in search paraphrase is NOT traceable to a primary source — excluded). Model DLRs as ~1:1 with submit_sm when requested, plus headroom for the rare intermediate+final double receipt. Use a separate RX bind for DLRs.

TLS: terminate mTLS on port 2776 (TLS 1.3 carrier convention; 2775 = legacy plaintext) on both legs.
calibration:
How to read these anchors for a solo OSS portfolio v1 — what reads as impressive-but-honest vs overreach, and where the real flex lives.

THE REAL FLEX IS CONCURRENCY/RESOURCE (via virtual threads), NOT THROUGHPUT. The user's thesis — 'VT craft = low resource consumption at high concurrency' — IS supported by the anchors: JEP 444 (1M VT supported; VTs exist for scale not speed), pkolaczk (Java VT at 1M tasks beat Go ~2x on memory, sub-GB), chrisgleissner/loom-webflux (VT-Netty on JDK 25 held 60K simultaneous connections with zero errors where WebFlux degraded). That is the headline craft story. BUT state the honest caveat plainly: SMPP production only needs 2-4 binds per system_id (tens-hundreds total), so demonstrating 10K+ idle socket pairs is a CAPABILITY/craft statement, not a production necessity. Conflating the two would read as overreach.

THROUGHPUT — impressive-but-honest band is 10K-25K submit_sm/sec end-to-end (relay, mTLS both legs, OIDC cached), NOT higher. Reasoning: smpp-core's 25K (single-author, no TLS, single leg) and emgload's ~25K (native C) converge as the modern SMPP ceiling; MockServer (mature Netty app on 6 cores) saturates ~36K req/s with real per-request work. Below ~10K reads as undertuned. Above ~50K end-to-end without a published percentile-table harness reads as overreach — every published JVM SMPP number above 25K is CODEC-ONLY (no network), and conflating codec ops/s (1.5-1.8M) with relay msg/s is the #1 trap to avoid. The codec microbench (1M+ ops/s, ~500-700 ns) is a separate, legitimately impressive artifact — present it as JMH single-core no-I/O, never as the relay number.

LATENCY — never promise sub-ms BIND latency; the bind path is TLS + OIDC and is RTT-bound. Honest target is 'p99 bind <= ~250 ms warm, <= ~2 s cold-path with fail-closed timeout.' Steady-state PER-PDU added latency CAN honestly be sub-ms (codec ~1 us + splice). Prefer local JWT (cached JWKS, ~1-5 ms) over remote introspection (~50-200 ms warm) for the bind path.

METHODOLOGY IS THE BAR (chrisgleissner/loom-webflux is the 2026 reference): disclose exact CPU model + core count + RAM + heap, exact JDK distro/build (Corretto 25.0.3 etc.), host rebooted before each run, co-location disclosed and justified, full sysctl/file-limit tuning shown, saturation knee AND failure modes reported (not hidden), percentile table (p50/p99/p99.99/max) not just average, open-model load (no coordinated omission), load generator on SEPARATE cores, reproducible command. Always pair a peak number with payload size (short_message bytes) + mTLS cipher + single-instance qualifier. Mark every number with its conditions; where a number cannot be sourced (mTLS overhead, two-leg relay throughput, idle-connection CPU), MEASURE it and label it 'self-measured' rather than borrowing a stray figure.

CAVEAT TO STATE EXPLICITLY in any portfolio write-up: every published JVM SMPP number above 25K/sec is codec-only (no network), and the only end-to-end JVM number (smpp-core's 25K) comes from a single-author project with no third-party replication. Setting a v1 target in the 10K-25K end-to-end / 10^5.5-10^6 codec range is defensible; claiming anything higher requires Companions to run its own JMH + loopback benchmark — which is itself a recommended portfolio artifact (the harness and saturation curve are more impressive than any single peak number).

DO NOT BORROW: the '~70 msg/s jSMPP' figure (unsourced competitor marketing), the 'Cloudhopper 10-100K msg/s' figure (generic SMS-topology marketing text from a cached gist, not a measurement), the '10K-100K Netty req/s' range (2012-2014 anecdote, meaningless without workload), or Aeron/Kafka ceilings (6-20M msg/s — UDP/IPC or 3-node cluster, not a TCP proxy; anchoring an SMPP relay to them would be overreach).
